content:
Consider this:

def my_const (x : Nat) (_ : Nat) := x

partial def f (x : Nat) : Nat := my_const 1 (f (x + 1))

#eval f 2

This #eval returns 1, but according to strict semantics, it should not. I believe this is a bug (or alternatively the reference should explicitly document that Lean is not guaranteed to be strict language in presence of partial definitions).
Context: https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/issues/13518
(nomeata said that I should avoid posting bug reports to bug tracker and use Zulip instead, so here I am.)

The compiler does not preserve non-termination in its optimization passes. The reference manual currently says almost nothing about the compiler. Is there a specific statement in the reference that implies that the compiler should preserve non-termination?

Julia Markus Himmel said:

Is there a specific statement in the reference that implies that the compiler should preserve non-termination?

I think yes. 4.1.1 says: "When the function is applied, the result is found by β-reduction: substituting the argument for the bound variable. In compiled code, this happens strictly: the argument must already be a value"

Would you be happy with the fix "In compiled code, this usually happens strictly"? As far as I know, the compiler pretty much only guarantees that if it returns a value x and you can prove that the function returns a value y that then x = y (assuming that you don't abuse unsafe or @[implemented_by] or use non-standard axioms etc.)

Robin Arnez said:

Would you be happy with the fix "In compiled code, this usually happens strictly"?

I think the reference should be as explicit as possible. I think it should say something like this (assuming this is true, of course):

In compiled code, this _usually_ happens strictly
Compiler is allowed to turn terminating code into non-terminating and vice-versa

Also, my example should be shown with comment "This code is allowed to return 1"

Robin Arnez said:

and these semantics for partial functions

As well as I understand, this code fragment applies to partial and unsafe functions only. But I can trigger that behavior without partial and unsafe functions so:

@[wf_preprocess]
def my_const (x : Nat) (_ : Nat) := x

def f (x : Nat) : Nat := my_const 1 (f (x + 1))

#eval f 2

(this code returns 1, too)
My idea is that this is not a section about compilation and thus longer elaboration on this wouldn't fit there
So maybe the best course of action is just to remove that sentence
I still think that the reference should warn user about this behavior somewhere. This behavior is surprising, and so should be explicitly documented

As well as I understand, the code you gave ( https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/45bdae81c924753c2bc3d870992c3c90bbc880e3/src/Lean/Compiler/LCNF/Basic.lean#L974-L990 ) assumes that functions marked as "unsafe" and "partial" may be non-terminating, and all other functions guaranteed to terminate. But this is not true, see my @[wf_preprocess] example above. So, this safe : Bool := true fragment seems to be buggy, i. e. it relies on wrong assumptions

Askar Safin said:

As well as I understand, this code fragment applies to partial and unsafe functions only. But I can trigger that behavior without partial and unsafe functions so:

@[wf_preprocess]
def my_const (x : Nat) (_ : Nat) := x

def f (x : Nat) : Nat := my_const 1 (f (x + 1))

#eval f 2

(this code returns 1, too)

The warning is already there on docs#Lean.Parser.Attr.wf_preprocess

Chris C said:

The warning is already there

My point is: comment in https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/45bdae81c924753c2bc3d870992c3c90bbc880e3/src/Lean/Compiler/LCNF/Basic.lean#L974-L990 implies that safe is set if and only if function is unsafe or partial. But this wf_preprocess means that other functions can be unsafe too (here I use word "unsafe" in sense "non-terminating"). So that code (i. e. https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/45bdae81c924753c2bc3d870992c3c90bbc880e3/src/Lean/Compiler/LCNF/Basic.lean#L974-L990 ) is buggy (assuming that its comment is correct)
I mean it is assumed that wf_preprocess simps don't actually change runtime behavior. In this sense, wf_preprocess can be consider unsafe (if used incorrectly).

Robin Arnez said:

can be consider unsafe

Yes, this is what I'm talking about. Using wf_preprocess should set that "safe" field to "false". Otherwise there is no sense in that "safe" field at all
No my idea is that using the wf_preprocess attribute puts the responsibility to the user to make sure there is no semantic change that would need safe := false.
But @Joachim Breitner will probably know better
In the same sense partial and unsafe put some responsibility on user
